opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think data is really the core bottleneck in robotics right now. Language models had the entire internet to learn from, but for robots there's no equivalent. Every piece of robot data has to be collected physically: someone teleoperates a robot, the robot does a task, and you record it. It's slow, it's expensive, and it doesn't scale the way text or images do.

What makes it worse is that the robotics field is very fragmented in terms of hardware. You have different arms, different grippers, bimanual platforms, humanoids. Historically, data collected on one robot was mostly useful only for that robot. If you trained on an ALOHA platform, that knowledge didn't transfer cleanly to a Franka arm or to a humanoid like Apollo. So the already-scarce data got split into even smaller islands.

Motion Transfer is our attempt to break down those islands. The idea is that the model learns a more unified understanding of motion and of how actions affect the physical world, across different embodiments. Instead of treating each robot's data as a separate dataset, the model learns from all of them together and figures out what's shared underneath. Things like how to approach an object, how to grasp it, what it means to open a drawer or hand something over. Those concepts are largely embodiment-independent, even if the exact joint commands are very different.

What we found in Gemini Robotics 1.5 was that this works surprisingly well. A skill demonstrated only on one robot can show up on another robot that never saw data for that task. So you get something close to zero-shot transfer of skills across embodiments. That effectively multiplies your data: every new demonstration on any platform benefits all the others.

I'd also say it changes how we think about scaling. Before, if you wanted a new robot to be capable, you had to start data collection almost from scratch. Now a new embodiment can piggyback on everything the model has already learned from other robots, and you need much less platform-specific data to get it going.

It doesn't fully solve the data problem. We still need more and more diverse data, and things like simulation, human videos, and better collection tools all matter. But Motion Transfer makes every bit of data we collect go much further, and I think that's a big step toward a truly general-purpose robot foundation model.

r001.rationale: The response says data from one robot was “mostly useful only for that robot” and did not transfer cleanly, but does not state that changing hardware makes the data unusable.

r002.rationale: The response says a skill demonstrated on one robot can appear on another robot with a different embodiment that had no data for that task.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that data scarcity in robotics is really a scarcity of transferable experience, not just a shortage of raw demonstrations. In language and vision we had the entire internet. In robotics, every demonstration is expensive. You need a physical robot, a teleoperator, a real environment, and you get maybe a few hundred episodes a day. And what's worse, that data has historically been locked to the embodiment it was collected on. Data from a two-arm ALOHA setup didn't help your Apollo humanoid very much, because the action spaces, the kinematics, and even the camera viewpoints are all different.

Motion Transfer is our attempt to break that lock. The core idea is that a lot of the knowledge inside a manipulation skill is actually embodiment-agnostic. How to approach an object, how to grasp a handle, how to pour without spilling, what the physical consequences of your actions are. Those are shared across robots. What differs is the low-level mapping from intent to joint commands. So instead of treating each robot's data as a separate island, we train on the pooled data from all our embodiments, and the model learns an internal representation of motion that abstracts away from the specific body, then grounds it back into the target robot's action space.

The practical effect is that skills learned on one robot show up on another with zero or very little additional data. We've seen behaviors that were only ever demonstrated on ALOHA appear on the Franka bi-arm, or on Apollo, when nobody collected those tasks for that platform. That's the thing that excites me most, because it changes the economics. Every new episode we collect on any robot now benefits the whole fleet, rather than just that one body. You get a kind of multiplier on your data.

I'd also say it pairs naturally with the other two pieces of 1.5. The embodied reasoning model handles high-level planning and spatial understanding, which is largely learned from web-scale data, so it isn't bottlenecked by robot data at all. And the thinking-before-acting behavior in the VLA lets the model decompose a long task into steps it already knows how to execute. So Motion Transfer sits at the low level, widening the pool of physical skills, while the reasoning layer stretches how far each skill can be reused.

I don't want to overclaim. Transfer isn't perfect, and the harder the dexterity requirement, the more the specific embodiment matters. But the direction is clear to me. We're moving from a world where every robot needs its own dataset to one where robots learn from each other, and that's probably the most important lever we have against the data problem.

r001.rationale: The response says data was historically “locked” to its original embodiment and that ALOHA data did not help Apollo “very much.” It does not clearly state that changing hardware makes previously collected data unusable.

r002.rationale: The response says Motion Transfer lets skills demonstrated on ALOHA appear on the Franka bi-arm or Apollo, including tasks never collected for those platforms.

astra-6.text:
I think the key idea is to make the data we already have useful across more robots. Robot experience is expensive to collect, and if every new robot needs its own dataset from scratch, that becomes a major bottleneck.

Motion Transfer addresses that by allowing experience collected on one robot to help train another robot with a different body. The goal isn’t simply to copy joint movements, because those can be very different. It’s to transfer the useful structure of the behavior while adapting how it’s executed.

That can reduce the amount of data you need to collect for each new platform. It doesn’t eliminate the need for robot-specific training and validation, but it makes existing experience go further. That’s an important direction for scaling robot learning.

r001.rationale: The response says data from one robot can help train another and reduce per-platform data collection. It does not say that changing hardware makes previously collected data unusable.

r002.rationale: The response says Motion Transfer lets experience from one robot help train a robot with a different body, adapting how the behavior is executed.

sol-6.1.text:
One of the challenges in robotics is that collecting data on a real robot is expensive, and that data is often specific to the robot that collected it. If every new robot has to learn everything from scratch, scaling becomes very difficult.

The idea behind Motion Transfer is to let a robot benefit from experience collected on other robot bodies. The exact joint movements may be different, but the underlying skill—reaching for an object, grasping it, or placing it somewhere—has a lot in common. Transferring that knowledge makes the available data useful across more robots.

So it doesn’t eliminate the need for robot training data, but it helps us get more value out of what we collect. That can reduce how much new data we need for each platform and make it easier to bring learned skills to new robots.

r001.rationale: The response says data is often robot-specific and new robots may otherwise need to learn from scratch, but it does not state that changing a robot’s hardware makes previously collected data unusable.

r002.rationale: It says Motion Transfer lets a robot benefit from experience collected on other robot bodies and transfer shared skills across robots with different movements.
